children.name: Operating Systems (OS Environments)
children.description: The primary software environment that manages computer hardware resources, provides common services for application programs, and presents a user interface.

children.title: General-Purpose Operating Systems (GPOS)
children.summary: Flexible operating systems built to run a wide variety of everyday programs, including web browsers, office tools, media players, and games, on standard hardware.

children.title: Commercial Proprietary Ecosystems
children.summary: Closed-source operating systems developed by a single vendor for commercial hardware.

children.title: Windows 11
children.summary: Microsoft’s flagship desktop OS. It dominates desktop computing globally with vast enterprise and PC gaming support.

children.title: macOS
children.summary: Apple’s proprietary desktop OS. It is deeply integrated with Apple hardware, favored for creative workflows and developer environments.

children.title: Open-Source Linux Distributions
children.summary: Operating systems built on the open-source Linux kernel paired with desktop graphical environments.

children.title: Ubuntu Desktop
children.summary: A user-friendly open-source Linux distribution. Popular for software development, customization, and workstations.

children.title: Fedora Workstation
children.summary: A community-driven distribution backed by Red Hat. Integrates cutting-edge Linux features and developer tools.

children.title: Arch Linux
children.summary: A lightweight, rolling-release Linux distribution. Highly customizable, allowing power users to build systems from the ground up.

children.title: BSD / Unix-Derived Desktops
children.summary: Independent open-source operating systems derived directly from original Research Unix codebases.

children.title: FreeBSD (Desktop configuration)
children.summary: An advanced Unix-like operating system. Known for networking performance, storage (ZFS), and system stability.

children.title: GhostBSD
children.summary: A desktop-oriented distribution based on FreeBSD. Offers a user-friendly Unix desktop out of the box.

children.title: Open-Source Base with Commercial Runtime
children.summary: Systems built on an open-source core paired with proprietary services and app ecosystems.

children.title: Android (Google Play Stack)
children.summary: Google’s mobile OS built on the Linux kernel. Powers the majority of global smartphones with an expansive app library.

children.title: Samsung One UI
children.summary: A customized Android interface created by Samsung. Adds multitasking capabilities and device ecosystem features.

children.title: Vertically Integrated Closed Platforms
children.summary: Proprietary hardware and software built exclusively for a single device ecosystem.

children.title: Apple iOS
children.summary: Apple’s mobile OS designed specifically for iPhone hardware. Highly optimized, secure, and tightly linked to Apple's app ecosystem.

children.title: iPadOS
children.summary: Apple's specialized tablet OS based on iOS. Tailored for larger screens, stylus input, and tablet productivity.

children.title: Independent / Community Mobile Platforms
children.summary: Pure open-source mobile environments created to run standard Linux software on smartphones.

children.title: PostmarketOS
children.summary: A real Linux distribution adapted for mobile phones. Extends the lifespan of older smartphone hardware.

children.title: Ubuntu Touch
children.summary: A mobile version of the Ubuntu OS. Offers a desktop-like convergent Linux environment on mobile hardware.

children.title: Enterprise Supported Linux
children.summary: Commercial Linux releases backed by paid corporate security updates, technical support, and compliance guarantees.

children.title: Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL)
children.summary: The leading enterprise commercial Linux OS. Provides corporate data centers with mission-critical stability and support.

children.title: SUSE Linux Enterprise Server (SLES)
children.summary: A major European enterprise Linux platform. Widely deployed for SAP applications and high-performance computing clusters.

children.title: Community Open-Source Server Linux
children.summary: Free, community-maintained Linux operating systems optimized for web servers and cloud infrastructure.

children.title: Ubuntu Server
children.summary: A widely used free Linux server distribution. The default standard for public cloud instances and web hosting.

children.title: Debian
children.summary: An extremely stable, community-governed Linux OS. Renowned for rock-solid stability and low system requirements.

children.title: Rocky Linux
children.summary: A community enterprise operating system designed to be downstream binary-compatible with RHEL. Provides a free alternative to commercial enterprise Linux.

children.title: Proprietary Commercial Server OS
children.summary: Enterprise platforms integrating tightly with corporate directory services, storage networks, and legacy software.

children.title: Windows Server
children.summary: Microsoft’s enterprise server operating system. Powers corporate networks, Active Directory user management, and corporate databases.

children.title: Oracle Solaris
children.summary: A Unix-based commercial server OS. Built for high-volume database workloads and legacy enterprise infrastructure.

children.title: Real-Time Operating Systems (RTOS)
children.summary: Operating systems where speed and precise timing are critical. An RTOS is designed to ensure tasks complete within defined timing constraints.

children.title: Mission-Critical Safety-Certified OS
children.summary: Systems where missing a timing deadline can cause total system failure or physical damage.

children.title: VxWorks
children.summary: A real-time OS designed for mission-critical embedded systems. Powers aerospace systems, Mars rovers, and defense hardware where failure is not an option.

children.title: Green Hills INTEGRITY
children.summary: A high-security real-time operating system. Certified for military aircraft, medical devices, and nuclear facility control.

children.title: PikeOS
children.summary: A real-time operating system with built-in virtualization. Isolates critical avionics software from non-critical sub-systems on airplanes.

children.title: Safety-Critical Automotive & Industrial OS
children.summary: Specialized operating systems designed for vehicle safety systems and manufacturing automation.

children.title: QNX Neutrino
children.summary: A commercial real-time microkernel OS. Controls modern automotive ADAS driving hardware, braking, and digital cockpits.

children.title: SafeRTOS
children.summary: A safety-critical RTOS pre-certified for international safety standards. Used in medical and industrial embedded systems.

children.title: AUTOSAR OS
children.summary: A standardized automotive real-time software architecture. Provides a common platform for electronic control units (ECUs) across car manufacturers.

children.title: Microcontroller / IoT Schedulers
children.summary: Ultra-lightweight real-time operating systems and schedulers built to run on small microcontrollers with minimal battery power and memory.

children.title: FreeRTOS
children.summary: A popular open-source real-time operating system kernel managed by AWS. Runs on IoT devices, microcontrollers, and smart sensors.

children.title: Zephyr RTOS
children.summary: An open-source, security-focused RTOS hosted by the Linux Foundation. Popular in wearable devices and low-power wireless nodes.

children.title: RT-Thread
children.summary: An open-source real-time operating system tailored for IoT hardware. Provides modular components such as GUI tools and networking stacks for microcontrollers.

children.title: Real-Time Kernel Patches
children.summary: Standard general-purpose operating system kernels modified to execute soft real-time tasks.

children.title: Linux with PREEMPT_RT patch
children.summary: A kernel modification that improves Linux determinism and latency. Used in industrial robotics and other applications where predictable response times are required.

children.title: Xenomai
children.summary: A real-time development framework for Linux. Executes precise motor control routines alongside standard Linux applications.

children.title: Embedded & Smart Device Operating Systems
children.summary: Lightweight operating systems embedded inside dedicated hardware devices such as smart TVs, appliances, automotive units, or routers.

children.title: Smart TV & Home Appliance Platforms
children.summary: Media-focused operating systems engineered for streaming applications and smart home interfaces.

children.title: LG webOS
children.summary: LG’s smart television operating system. Provides a graphical interface for smart TVs and connected appliances.

children.title: Samsung Tizen
children.summary: An open-source Linux-based OS backed by Samsung. Powers smart televisions, displays, and home appliances.

children.title: Android TV
children.summary: A version of Android optimized for media devices. Gives smart TVs and streaming devices access to the Google Play ecosystem.

children.title: In-Vehicle Infotainment (IVI)
children.summary: Operating systems controlling dashboard screens, cabin environmental controls, and navigation.

children.title: Android Automotive OS (AAOS)
children.summary: A full Android OS embedded directly into vehicle hardware. Controls cabin infotainment and vehicle settings without requiring a connected phone.

children.title: Automotive Grade Linux (AGL)
children.summary: An open-source collaborative project building a shared Linux system for cars. Allows automakers to build custom dashboard experiences without starting from scratch.

children.title: Enterprise Switch & Router OS
children.summary: Operating systems built to route network traffic, manage firewall rules, and maintain high-speed network connections.

children.title: Cisco IOS / IOS-XE
children.summary: Cisco’s proprietary network hardware operating system. Widely deployed across enterprise routers and network switches.

children.title: Juniper Junos OS
children.summary: Juniper Networks' FreeBSD-based operating system. Powers network infrastructure including internet service provider routers.

children.title: Arista EOS
children.summary: A Linux-based network operating system. Powers high-speed data center switches for cloud providers and financial networks.

children.title: Consumer & Edge Router Firmware
children.summary: Minimal operating systems and firmware configured for home Wi-Fi routers and local network hardware.

children.title: OpenWrt
children.summary: An open-source Linux distribution for embedded network devices. Replaces basic router firmware to add advanced networking features and security.

children.title: DD-WRT
children.summary: A third-party Linux-based firmware for wireless routers. Boosts home router functionality and adds features such as VPN support.

children.title: OPNsense
children.summary: An open-source, FreeBSD-based firewall and routing platform. Provides advanced firewall and network-management tools for small businesses and home labs.

children.title: Cloud-Native & Container Operating Systems
children.summary: Stripped-down operating systems designed specifically to run inside cloud data centers and serve as hosts for isolated software containers such as Docker and Kubernetes.

children.title: Immutable Linux Hosts
children.summary: Read-only or minimally mutable operating systems built primarily to run containers and update automatically.

children.title: Talos Linux
children.summary: A Linux distribution built explicitly for Kubernetes. Managed entirely via an API and designed without traditional SSH-based administration.

children.title: Flatcar Container Linux
children.summary: A community-driven, immutable Linux distribution. Serves as a low-maintenance host for large-scale container deployments.

children.title: Fedora CoreOS
children.summary: An automatically updating, container-focused operating system. Combines an immutable-style system with container optimization.

children.title: AWS Bottlerocket
children.summary: An open-source, Linux-based operating system built by Amazon Web Services. Designed to reduce maintenance and security exposure when running container workloads.

children.title: Minimalist Application Base Images
children.summary: Lightweight operating system templates and runtime base images used inside containers to keep cloud software small and efficient.

children.title: Micro-Distributions
children.summary: Lightweight system environments used inside container images to keep cloud software fast and minimize unnecessary components.

children.title: Alpine Linux
children.summary: A security-oriented, ultra-lightweight Linux distribution commonly used as a base for small container images.

children.title: BusyBox
children.summary: Software that combines tiny versions of many common Unix utilities into a single executable. Provides basic terminal tools inside minimal containers and embedded systems.

children.title: Google Distroless
children.summary: Minimal container base images containing an application runtime and required dependencies without traditional package managers or shells.

children.title: Wearable & Spatial Computing Operating Systems
children.summary: Operating systems engineered for body-worn technology such as smartwatches, fitness trackers, and AR/VR headsets requiring small screen formats, sensor tracking, and low power usage.

children.title: Smartwatch & Fitness OS
children.summary: Compact operating systems tuned for wrist-sized displays, biometric tracking, and wireless synchronization.

children.title: Apple watchOS
children.summary: Apple’s proprietary smartwatch operating system. Offers app integration and health tracking for the Apple Watch ecosystem.

children.title: Wear OS by Google
children.summary: An Android platform variant designed for smartwatches. Powers watches across multiple hardware brands.

children.title: Garmin OS
children.summary: A lightweight proprietary operating system optimized for battery life and endurance sports tracking.

children.title: 3D / Headset OS
children.summary: Operating systems built for spatial computing headsets that map physical environments, track movement, and render interactive visual content.

children.title: Apple visionOS
children.summary: Apple’s spatial operating system for Vision Pro. Blends digital media with the real world using eye tracking and hand gestures.

children.title: Meta Horizon OS
children.summary: Meta’s Android-derived spatial operating system. Powers Meta Quest headsets and their associated VR ecosystem.

children.title: Enterprise Infrastructure & Mainframe Operating Systems
children.summary: High-capacity operating systems designed to run on enterprise mainframes and large-scale infrastructure, supporting high-volume transactions and databases with high availability.

children.title: High-Volume Transaction Mainframes
children.summary: Enterprise platforms built to process extremely large transaction workloads with high reliability.

children.title: IBM z/OS
children.summary: IBM’s flagship mainframe operating system. Supports large-scale transaction processing and enterprise workloads.

children.title: IBM z/VM
children.summary: A mainframe virtualization operating system that allows mainframes to run multiple virtual guest systems simultaneously.

children.title: IBM z/VSE
children.summary: A mainframe operating system designed for transaction-processing workloads and enterprise applications.

children.title: Clustered & Network-Transparent Systems
children.summary: Systems engineered to coordinate independent networked computers so they can operate as an integrated computing environment.

children.title: Plan 9 from Bell Labs
children.summary: A research operating system developed at Bell Labs as a successor to Unix. Represented system resources, devices, and network connections through a unified file-oriented interface.

children.title: Amoeba
children.summary: A distributed research operating system that explored combining a network of workstations into an integrated computing environment.

children.title: Kernels
children.subtitle: Hardware Management
children.summary: The core program that mediates between hardware and every other layer of software.

children.title: Monolithic
children.subtitle: Single high-privileged memory space
children.summary: All operating system processes, drivers, and file systems run inside a single, high-privileged memory space. Split by how they handle code loading.

children.title: Static Monolithic
children.summary: The entire kernel and all supported hardware drivers are compiled into one unchangeable binary file. Adding a new driver or changing a core service requires recompiling the entire kernel from scratch.

children.title: Traditional UNIX (System V / Early BSD)
children.summary: The grandfather of modern operating systems. Hardware drivers, network protocols, and file systems were welded into a single block of code. Adding new hardware required manually rewriting the source code and rebuilding the entire system.

children.title: MS-DOS
children.summary: The ultimate simple monolith. It featured absolutely no separation or interior walls between user applications and the core operating system, meaning a single bug in any program would instantly crash the whole machine.

children.title: Early Linux (Pre-1995)
children.summary: The original versions of Linux. Before loadable modules were invented, if you bought a new sound card, you had to manually download its driver code, paste it into the core operating system files, and recompile the entire OS from scratch to use it.

children.title: IBM z/TPF
children.summary: A specialized ultra-fast system used by airlines and credit card networks. It runs everything in one single, raw memory space with no modular overhead, allowing it to handle millions of real-time transactions per second without slowing down.

children.title: XTS-400
children.summary: A high-assurance, military-grade operating system. It uses a rigid, unchangeable static layout so security engineers can thoroughly audit every single line of code, ensuring absolutely no hidden loopholes or modifications can be sneaked in later.

children.title: Embedded RTOS (Real-Time Operating Systems)
children.summary: The fixed software baked onto chips inside microwaves, anti-lock car brakes, or digital watches. Because these devices only perform one specific job, the kernel is permanently written at the factory, never updates, and runs instantly.

children.title: Modular Monolithic
children.summary: The system still operates in a unified, high-privileged supervisor mode, but can dynamically load or unload blocks of code — Loadable Kernel Modules (LKMs) — at runtime to support new hardware or filesystems without rebooting.

children.title: Modern Linux
children.summary: Ubuntu, Debian, Red Hat — modular monolithic kernel.

children.title: FreeBSD
children.summary: A modular monolithic kernel example.

children.title: Hybrid
children.subtitle: Microkernel design, monolithic execution
children.summary: An architectural compromise that maps components like a microkernel but runs them inside a single monolithic address space to eliminate performance-slowing IPC message overhead. Split by structural composition.

children.title: Subsystem-Based Hybrids
children.summary: Isolates modular operational subsystems (like the graphics rendering manager or networking layers) inside high-privilege execution modes for maximum execution speed.

children.title: Windows NT Kernel
children.summary: Powers Windows 10 and Windows 11.

children.title: Composite / Co-Kernels
children.summary: Fuses two completely different operating system architectures directly together into a single running entity.

children.title: Apple XNU Kernel
children.summary: Powers macOS and iOS. Bridges a Mach microkernel structure together with a monolithic FreeBSD subsystem.

children.title: Microkernel
children.subtitle: Minimal core, services in user space
children.summary: The kernel is stripped down to the near-minimum code required to handle thread scheduling, virtual memory mapping, and messaging primitives. Traditional services like device drivers and file systems are kicked out into isolated user spaces. Split by design generation.

children.title: First-Generation Microkernels
children.summary: Early versions where sending data back and forth between isolated user-space processes (IPC) suffered from heavy performance overhead and slowdowns.

children.title: Early Mach
children.summary: e.g. Mach 3.0 — first-generation microkernel example.

children.title: Early Chorus
children.summary: A first-generation microkernel example.

children.title: Second-Generation Microkernels
children.summary: Redesigned from scratch to make IPC memory-page mapping fast and lightweight, with many versions formally verified for bulletproof security.

children.title: L4 Microkernel Family
children.summary: A second-generation microkernel family.

children.title: seL4
children.summary: A formally verified microkernel.

children.title: Minix 3
children.summary: A second-generation microkernel example.

children.title: QNX
children.summary: Widely deployed in automotive systems.

children.title: Nanokernel
children.subtitle: Extreme minimalism
children.summary: An extreme variation of a microkernel shrunk down to near-total minimalism, running in privileged hardware mode to offer basic hardware timing or instruction surfaces. Classified by implementation type.

children.title: HAL / Virtualization Nanokernels
children.summary: A thin software layer that handles nothing but hardware interrupt clocks and resource mapping. Often sits underneath a normal operating system to inject real-time responsiveness into it.

children.title: KeyKOS
children.summary: A HAL/virtualization nanokernel example.

children.title: Adeos
children.summary: A virtualization layer nanokernel example.

children.title: Classic PowerPC Mac OS Nanokernel
children.summary: Versions 7 through 9, handled 68k software emulation underneath.

children.title: Exokernel
children.subtitle: Protection separated from management
children.summary: An experimental paradigm that completely separates resource protection from resource management. Forces no high-level virtual abstractions (like files or directories) on developers. Defined by their reliance on application libraries.

children.title: Library Operating System (LibOS) Abstraction
children.summary: The exokernel acts strictly as a thin security guard verifying who owns a raw disk sector or memory address. Applications link directly to unprivileged libraries (Library Operating Systems) containing only the specific filesystem or network code they choose.

children.title: MIT Exokernel Projects
children.summary: XOK, Aegis — MIT exokernel research projects.

children.title: JOS
children.summary: A LibOS-abstraction exokernel example.

children.title: Nemesis
children.summary: A LibOS-abstraction exokernel example.

children.title: Unikernel
children.subtitle: App compiled with minimal system functions
children.summary: A model built upon library operating system concepts where application code is compiled directly with minimal system functions into a single, specialized, bootable binary image meant to run on a cloud hypervisor. Split by compliance standards.

children.title: Clean-Slate / Language-Specific Unikernels
children.summary: Built entirely from scratch using type-safe languages. Ignore legacy Unix standards entirely, compiling only the exact lines of code needed to make a purpose-built program execute.

children.title: MirageOS
children.summary: OCaml-based unikernel.

children.title: HaLVM
children.summary: Haskell Lightweight Virtual Machine.

children.title: LING
children.summary: Erlang-based unikernel.

children.title: Generalized / Legacy POSIX-Compliant Unikernels
children.summary: Built with backward compatibility in mind. Include a thin translation layer to simulate traditional operating system pathways, allowing standard, unmodified applications written in C, C++, or Java to compile directly into a unikernel.

children.title: OSv
children.summary: A POSIX-compliant unikernel example.

children.title: Rumprun
children.summary: Uses NetBSD rump drivers to form a unikernel footprint.

children.title: Drawbridge
children.summary: A POSIX-compliant unikernel example.
